title: Effectiveness of an art therapy group intervention with elements of acceptance and commitment therapy to reduce psychological stress in people with a refugee background
summary:
People with refugee experience are often exposed to extreme stress, which can lead to post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), anxiety disorders or depressive symptoms. Traditional therapeutic approaches can be challenging in certain situations, particularly when language barriers or cultural differences influence psychotherapeutic work. This study examines the extent to which a combination of art therapy and acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) can represent an effective, culturally sensitive treatment approach for traumatized refugees. While art therapy uses non-verbal forms of expression to enable emotional processing, ACT offers a framework for acceptance and value orientation to strengthen psychological flexibility and resilience. Using a mixed-methods design, quantitative and qualitative data will be collected to evaluate the effectiveness of this combined intervention. The results are intended to provide evidence-based recommendations for therapeutic practice with refugees. 
The mental health of people with refugee experience is one of the most pressing social challenges of today. Many refugees are in theirs country of origin or during the escape massive traumatic experiences such as war, been subjected to persecution or torture. After arriving in a safe country, they continue to face numerous psychosocial stresses, including uncertain immigration status, isolation and discrimination. These factors make it more difficult to process traumatic experiences and increase the risk of mental illness. At the same time, studies show that classic trauma therapy approaches are not equally effective for all refugees. Language barriers, cultural differences in the perception of trauma and the stigma towards psychotherapeutic support make it difficult to use conventional treatment methods. Therefore, there is an urgent need for alternative, culturally sensitive therapeutic approaches adapted to the specific needs of this population. As a non-verbal form of therapy, art therapy offers a promising opportunity to enable emotional processing without linguistic hurdles. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) complements this approach by strengthening psychological flexibility, contributing to the acceptance of stressful emotions, and supporting affected individuals in leading a values-based life despite difficult experiences. The combination of these two approaches could represent an innovative and effective form of trauma treatment for refugees.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Adults with a refugee background who came to Germany within the last 5 years between the ages of 18 and 39
Exclusion criteria:
Acute psychosis, suicidality, severe cognitive impairment
